reference.source: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
clinicalPearls: The most common type of childhood exotropia: an intermittent outward deviation controlled by fusion much of the time that breaks down with fatigue, illness, inattention or distance fixation
Classic history is of one eye drifting outward when the child is tired or daydreaming, with characteristic closure or squinting of one eye in bright sunlight
It is often more manifest for distance than near and is classified by the distance-near relationship into basic, divergence-excess/pseudo-divergence-excess, and convergence-insufficiency types

Control is assessed clinically and graded (for example with the Newcastle Control Score), using spontaneous control, recovery after cover and the frequency of manifest deviation to guide management and the timing of surgery
Because binocular single vision is present for much of the time, amblyopia is less common than in constant strabismus, but binocular function and stereopsis should be monitored

Management ranges from observation, refractive correction, orthoptic convergence exercises and part-time occlusion to surgery (usually bilateral lateral rectus recession or a unilateral recess-resect) when control deteriorates
Diplopia is uncommon in children because they suppress, but adults with a decompensating exodeviation may report intermittent diplopia or asthenopia
Deterioration to a constant exotropia, reducing stereoacuity, or an increasing frequency or size of deviation are indications to intervene
reference.pathophysiology: Intermittent exotropia reflects an imbalance between an excessive tonic divergence position of the eyes and the fusional convergence mechanisms that normally maintain alignment. When fusional convergence is adequate the eyes stay straight; when fusional control is overcome, by fatigue, illness, inattention, bright light or dissociation under monocular or distance conditions, the latent exophoria becomes a manifest exotropia. The precise cause is not fully understood but involves anatomical and innervational factors and the balance between accommodative convergence and the resting divergent position. Over time control may deteriorate, with a longer duration of manifest deviation, suppression of the deviating eye and possible progression to a constant exotropia.
additionalDifferentials: Exophoria, which is fully compensated and never manifest
Sensory exotropia from monocular visual loss
Convergence insufficiency with a near exodeviation and a distinct near-distance pattern
Consecutive exotropia following previous esotropia surgery
Duane retraction syndrome type II or third nerve palsy
Neurological or internuclear causes of an exodeviation in acquired cases
additionalInvestigations: Prism cover test for distance and near, including with plus lenses or patching to unmask true divergence excess
Assessment and grading of control (for example the Newcastle Control Score)
Cycloplegic refraction and correction of significant refractive error
Stereoacuity and sensory or binocular function testing
Extended monocular occlusion to reveal the maximum deviation
Dilated fundus examination to exclude a sensory cause
redFlags: Acquired exotropia with neurological symptoms or signs
Reduced vision in one eye suggesting a sensory cause, requiring exclusion of organic pathology
Progression from an intermittent to a constant deviation with loss of stereopsis
New-onset diplopia in a child, which is uncommon and warrants investigation
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally good: many children maintain useful binocular vision and stereopsis, and surgery achieves satisfactory alignment in most, although under- and over-correction and recurrence occur and repeat surgery is sometimes needed. Binocular outcomes are best when good control and stereoacuity are preserved before intervention.
pitfalls: Measuring only the near angle and missing a distance or divergence-excess deviation (use prolonged occlusion and plus lenses)
Overlooking a small refractive error, including myopia, that affects control
Mistaking a constant sensory exotropia for the benign intermittent form
Operating too early or on poorly documented control, risking consecutive esotropia
Failing to monitor stereopsis and control over time
references: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
von Noorden's Binocular Vision and Ocular Motility
management: Correct significant refractive error after cycloplegic refraction with spectacles, including overminus lenses to stimulate accommodative convergence
Use non-surgical measures for well-controlled deviation: active observation, orthoptic convergence exercises and part-time occlusion
Treat any amblyopia with occlusion or penalisation of the dominant eye
Offer strabismus surgery, usually bilateral lateral rectus recession or a unilateral recess-resect, when control deteriorates or the deviation becomes frequent or constant
Monitor control (for example with the Newcastle Control Score), binocular single vision and stereoacuity to time intervention
Manage under paediatric ophthalmology and orthoptics, counselling on the possibility of under-correction, over-correction and recurrence requiring further surgery

nodes.text: Outward drift of one eye when tired, ill or fixating at distance
Neurological signs, reduced vision in one eye, loss of stereopsis or new diplopia?
Neuro-ophthalmic and sensory evaluation; neuroimaging if acquired
Prism cover test near and distance, cycloplegic refraction, control, stereoacuity
Intermittent pattern with good control and no sensory cause?
Consider constant or sensory exotropia; re-grade control
Correct significant refractive error with spectacles
Surgery when control deteriorates or deviation becomes frequent or constant
Monitor control, stereoacuity and binocular single vision
Control monitored; surgery timed by deterioration in control
